ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Currency management of RBI 
*221. SHRIMATI SARLA MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the growing menace of free How of 
counterfeit currency notes from across the borders, particularly Indo-Nepal 
Border; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard; 
(c) whether it is a fact that this has been the result of bad currency 
management of RBI; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken by Government to improve the currency 
management of RBI? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) Fake Indian Currency Notes (FICN) seized by the Police and recovered 
by the Banks since 1998 are as follows:—  
Notes Seized/Recovered
Year    
  Number Value (Rs. lakhs) 
1998  46,402 64.97 
1999  1,11,969 183.35 
2000  2,83,790 594.47 
2001 (upto June) 1,21,003 320.82 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2002] 
However, seizures/recoveries are an insignificant proportion of the total 
volume of genuine bank notes in circulation. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) There is no direct correlation betw een management of currency by the 
RBI and FICN. However, the Government has taken a number of steps to 
curb the menace of counterfeiting. These, inter-alia, include: 
 
(1) Incorporation of additional security features, particularly in the higher 
denomination notes. 
(2) Publicising security features through the print and electronic media. 
(3) Withdrawal of soiled notes from circulation for ensuring clean notes to 
the public. 
(4) Installation of Ultra Violet lamps in the public sector bank branches to 
enable easy detection of counterfeits.

*227. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the steps taken or proposed to be taken for encouraging 
export promotion in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that minimum five members should be allowed to 
go to foreign countries for export promotion development under Ministry's 
Market Development Authority; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether this would boost the export promotion activities; and 
(e) if not, whether Government will review this decision? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) Export promotion 
continues to be a major thrust area. Va rious measures to boost exports have 
been undertaken in order to provide competitive edge to the Indian goods in 
the International market which, inter alia, include the following: 
• Formulation of Medium Term Export Strategy for the period 2002—07, 
which gives a road map for export sector by setting a 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2002] 
target of achieving 1% of world exports (US$ 80 billion) by the year 
2007. 
• Reduction in the export credit rate for both pre-shipment and post-
shipment. 
• Social financial package to manufact urer exporters with an export 
contract of Rs. 100 crore or above for the period of one year. 
• Extension of the normal to repatriation period from 180 days to 360 
days for exports for a period of one year on exports made to Latin 
American countries. 
• Upward revision of duty drawback rates on a number of product groups. 
• Removal of restrictions for exports on a number of items. 
• Reduction in the transaction costs through decentralization and 
simplification of procedures. 
• Setting up of Special Economic Zones. 
• Setting up a Business Information and Facilitation Centre with a Trade 
Portal. 
• Woven segment of readymade garments has been de-reserved from the 
SSI sector. De-reservation of knitted segment has also been announced 
in the budget 2002-03. 
• Foreign equity participation upto 100% through automatic route has 
been allowed in the textile sector with certain exceptions. 
• Marketing Development Assistance (MDA) scheme simplified to the 
advantage of the exporters in undertaking market promotion activities 
abroad. 
• Launching Market Access Initiative scheme to give more thrust than in 
the past, in marketing our products to the global markets. 
(b) to   (e)   Under   the   MDA   scheme   guidelines,   there   is  no 
minimum requirement in terms of numbers for undertaking export 
16 

[19 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
promotion activities either by way of sale cum study tour or participation in 
fairs/exhibitions etc. However, these gu idelines stipulate that in respect of 
joint market promotion activities organized by the Export Promotion 
Councils etc., there should be a minimum participation of five exporters. This 
is considered necessary in order to ensure effective representation of the 
industry especially keeping in view the fact that such events involve 
additional expenditure from public funds in meeting the cost of visit of 
accompanying Council officials and other common activities. 
The entire thrust of the MDA scheme is to assist export promotion 
activities in partnership with the exporting community, and presently there is 
no proposal to review the guidelines stipulating participation of at least five 
exporters in market promotion activities organized by the Councils etc.,

*231. SHRI K.  KALAVENKATA RAO: DR. Y. 
LAKSHMI PRASAD: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether representatives of farmers' organizations have demanded that 
controls on movement of a farm products be removed and concessional 
import duty on farm machinery be levied; and 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2002] 
(b) if so, what is Government's reac tion thereto and the steps proposed to 
be taken in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N.RAMACHANDRAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Government have issued Order vide G.S.R. 104(E), dated the 15th 
February, 2002, under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 1955), to 
remove movement restrictions on Specified Foodstuffs, viz. wheat, 
paddy/rice, coarse grains, sugar, edible oilseeds and edible oils with effect 
from 17.3.2002. Government have also reduced the basic customs duty on 
agricultural machinery such as harvesters, machinery for soil preparation, 
machinery for grading, sorting of seeds, fruits, etc. and machinery for poultry 
keeping from 25% to 15% with effect from 1st March, 2002. 
SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Sir, the current import duty is 35 per

has reduced the basic customs duty on agricultural machinery from 25 per

is still excessive. I would like to know whether the Government has 
considered the demand of farmers' organizations for concessional imports 
duty on agricultural machinery used by th e farmers so that they are available

suggestions of the hon. Member. Th e Government may examine all these 
suggestions and take a decision.

whether the Government proposes to go in for the total decontrol of sugar

Government. We have said that we could go in for deregulation, but, this must 
be accompanied with a number of steps 
18 

[19 March, 2002]    RAJYA SABHA 
so that neither the sugar-mills nor the cane growers nor the 
consumers are inconvenienced. I have  already stated in the Budget 
that we are trying to build a future market for sugar. We are hoping 
that the future market will be ready sometime in October-November 
this year, and perhaps, that w ill be the occasion when decontrol 
could be taken up further. But I would like to inform the House, 
through you, Sir, that as a result of a number of steps which the 
Government has taken, sugar licencing is not a problem now. As far

cent of the production; and sugar prices are also steady in the 
market. So, we will proceed with deregulation in the sugar sector 
with a kind of caution that I have mentioned.

Losses suffered by IA due to aviation fuel 
1635. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian Ai rlines are incurring losses worth 
crores of Rupees on aviation fuel due to connivance between some officials 
of air traffic control and private airliners; 
(b) whether Government have received any such complaint; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the action taken by Government 
thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) There have been occasio ns when incoming flights were put 
to hold and departing aircraft made to wait at holding point for a longer 
period or desired flight levels not allocated to Indian Airlines flights by Air 
Traffic Control (ATC). This results in consumption of extra fuel. 
(b) and (c) The details of the three su ch instances which recently came to 
the notice of the Government were looked into. These details are as 
follows:— 
(i) A complaint was received through Press Clipping entitled "IA loss is 
ATC officials' gain" dated 7th January, 2002 of the Asian Age. It was 
alleged that ATC at Ahmedabad was having understanding with pilots of 
private airlines and the Indian Airlines ' flights are put "on hold" in the air. 
The matter has been investigated an d it was found that the complaint was 
baseless. Ahmedabad Airport is equipped with the state-of-art MSSR Radar. 
The traffic density at Ahmedabad Airport is very low and all the aircraft are 
p r o v i d e d  r a d a r  s e r v i c e s  b o t h  i n  t h e  A p p r o a c h     C o n t r o l     a n d     A r e a     
Control.    Ahmedabad    ATC    is 
50 

[19 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
maintaining safe, orderly and expeditious flow of air traffic. No complaint 
has, however, been received from any airlines in this regard. 
(ii) The other complaint was received from Indian Airlines that on 3rd 
January, 2002 at IGI Airport, Sahara Airlines flight 302 was given preference 
in departure over their flight IC-401. This has been investigated. The taxi 
routing of Sahara Airlines was shorter than the taxi routing of Indian Airlines 
flight IC-401. Sahara was cleared for departure first as it was to fly at higher 
level than Indian Airlines flight. This was done to facilitate maximum 
number of departures with least over all delay. 
(iii) Indian Airlines brought it to the notice of Airports Authority of India 
(AAI) that their aircraft operating f light IC-813 on 4.1.2002 was asked by 
Delhi ATC to hold position to adjust the departure of another flight. This 
matter has been enquired into. The factual position is that this incident 
involved Air India flight 316. Since Air India flight 316 was to fly at a higher 
level| Air India was allowed to depart ahead of Indian Airlines flight IC-813 
and they were both flying on the same route.

1652. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of

responsibility of enforcement of the TRIPS; and

TRIPS? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) to (b) TRIPS 
Agreement covers seven areas of Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) 
including plant veriety, protected in India by separate legislation. These Acts 
provide for civil and criminal remedies against infringement of these IPRs. 
For civil remedies, a right holder may file a suit in a court not inferior to a 
District Court having jurisdiction to try that suit in a manner specified in the 
concerned Act. Where there are provi sions for criminal remedies for 
infringement of IPRs like trademark, copyright, etc., a police officer-in-charge 
of a police station can investigate a case on his own when the commission of 
a cognizable offence is brought to this knowledge. In case of non-cognizable 
offences, the police can investigate only on order of a Magistrate having power 
to try such case. Enforcement of th e provisions dealing with criminal 
penalties is the responsibility of the State Governments through police force. 
Ministry of Human Resource Development has also taken several measures to 
strengthen enforcement of copyrights. These include setting up of copyright 
Enforcement Advisory Council, organization of seminarsAvorkshops to 
create greater awareness about copyright law among the enforcement 
personnel and general public, encouraging setting up of collective 
administrative societies, creation of  separate cells in State police 
headquarters, etc.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) According to 
the Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA), no disease 
spread was reported in the prawn hatc heries of Kerala after June 2001. 
However, they are aware of the outbreak of disease in prawn/shrimp farms of 
the State during January '02. The disease reportedly appeared in the 
traditional shrimp farms as isolated in cidences during late December 2001.

one of the main reasons for the outbreak is the failure of the farmers to adopt 
the basic management measures needed to avoid the infection and spread of 
the disease. Other responsible factors include water quality, soil condition, 
plankton blooms, weather conditions etc.

1677. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) RBI have revised the following 
money exchanging rules: 
1. Full Fledged Money Changers (FFMCs) 
(i) Since money changing is a fund based activity. with a view to ensuring 
that only credible players enter the field, Net Own Funds (NOF) for the 
FFMCs having multiple branches has been raised to Rs. 50 lakhs, a two year 
period will be allowed to the existing FFMCs for augmenting their NOF. 
(ii) Earlier, Travellers Cheques (T Cs) stocking arrangement with any TC 
issuing organization was a pre-condition for the issue of FFMC licence. This 
condition is withdrawn in order to  improve the encashment facilities 
available in the country. 
2. Restricted Money Changers (RMCs) 
Earlier, RMC lincences were issued by  Reserve Bank of India. Under the 
new Scheme announced by the Reserve Bank, Authorized Dealers and 
FFMCs have been accorded the freedom to enter into agency/franchising 
agreements for the purposes of carrying on RMC business, i.e. conversion of 
foreign currency notes or travellers cheques into rupees. Resident entities 
wishing to undertake restricted money changing would no longer be required 
to obtain RBI licence.

New auto fuel policy 
1732. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a new auto fuel policy based on 
recommendations of the R.A. Mashelkar Committee has been finalised;

undue haste without giving adequate opportunity to the affected interests to 
discuss and analyse the document? 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The broad recommendations made in the interim report of the 
Committee are:— 
1. The Auto Fuel Policy should be based on targeted vehicular emission 
standards for various categories of vehicles, allowing use of different 
technologies and fuels, which can meet the emission standards. 
2. In the developed world and elsewhere, vehicular emission standards 
and auto fuel quality necessary to meet the standards alone are 
prescribed, giving choice to the public, manufacturers, owners and 
operators of motor vehicles to choose the vehicle type and the fuel. The 
same policy be adopted for India. 
3. The following roadmap for implementation of vehicular emission norms 
and auto fuel quality be followed: 
(i) Bharat Stage-II norms which are in place in the four mega cities of 
Delhi. Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai should be introduced in the 
other three mega cities of Bangalore, Hyderabad and Ahmedabad 
as early as possible but not later than the end of 2003. 
(ii) Bharat Stage-II norms should be  introduced in the entire country 
from  1st April 2005. 
(iii) Euro-Ill equivalent emission norms for all categories of vehicles 
(excluding two and three wheelers), detailed by the Committee, 
should be introduced in seven mega cities from 1st April 2005. 
4. Low emission vehicles and the compatible fuels are not the only factors 
which would have a bearing on air quality. Other cost effective 
measures such as comprehensive in spection and certification system 
for in use vehicles with private sector participation, fitment of emission 
reduction devices in the existing vehicles, traffic management, 
construction of bye passes etc. should also be put in place. 
5. Upgraded    and    additional    emission    testing    facilities    and 
144 

[19 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
establishment of surveillance and checking of emission warranty 
 systems for new vehicles be set up. 
6. To put in place the new emissions norms, substantial investments need 
to be made to produce appropriate quality fuel and the vehicles. 
Preferential treatment to the oil and auto industry in matters relating to 
custom duty, excise duty, depreciation, soft-loans etc. need to be 
provided. 
7. In addition to petrol and diesel, Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and 
Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) are permitted to be used as auto fuels. The 
Government has futher decided to blend ethanol with petrol. CNG, LPG 
and other alternative fuels need to be encouraged, giving the choice of 
fuel and vehicle technology to the customers. Any combination of fuel 
and vehicle technology, which meets the prescribed emission norms should 
be acceptable. 
8. The fiscal regime applicable to the auto fuels should be directed towards 
achieving the economic pricing of various fuels, instead of  prsently 
prevailing distored pricing. This would help in long term planning and 
supply of quality products. 
(c) No. Sir.

Decline in per capita availability of water 
1770. SHRI DINA NATH MISHRA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the reasons for decline in the per capita availability of water 
in the country; 
(b) the steps Government are contem plating for a comprehensive and 
integrated approach to water management especially in the context of its 
demand; 
(c) if so, the details of measures proposed to be adopted by Government in 
this regard; and 
(d) whether there has been any evaluation of the previous national water 
policies to ascertain the causes responsible for the decline? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (d) The 
Average annual precipitation in the country remains more or less fixed 
according to the natural hydrologic cy cle. The per capita average annual 
water availability in the country is reducing progressively owing to increasing 
population. The average annual per capita water availability is estimated to be 
about 1829 Cu.m. in 2001 AD at national level. 
National Water Policy (1987) provides for integrated management of water 
resources with basin as a unit of development encouraging construction of 
major, medium and minor schemes. Water resources development is taken up 
by the State Governments according to this policy. In order to meet the 
growing demand of water, apart from medium and minor schemes, a live 
storage capacity of 177 BCM has been created by construction of large dams 
upto 1995. Projects to add in additional storage capacity of about 75 BCM 
are under construction and 132 BCM are under planning. The replenishable 
ground water is of the order of 432 BCM, out of which about 154 
180 

[19 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
BCM has been developed for use. With the help of these storages and other 
minor irrigation schemes an irrigation potential of about 100 Mha is likely to 
have been created by the end of the Ninth Plan against the ultimate irrigation 
potential of 139.9 Mha in the country. 
As a long term measure National Water Development Agency of Government of 
India have formulated National Perspective Plan for water resources development 
which envisages interlinking between various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan 
rivers for transfer of water from surp lus basins to wate r deficit basins. 
Government of India is also promoting rain water harvesting through Watershed 
Management Programme, artificial recharge of ground water and roof-top rain 
water harvesting under the sector reform project of Accelerated Rural Water 
Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural Development, for which 
technical and financial assistance is provided to the State Government and other 
implementing agencies. Central Ground Water Board has also taken up pilot 
studies for artificial ground water recharge. Assistance is also extended to 
State Governments under Command Area Development Programme for bridging 
the gap between potential created and utilised. For early completion of ongoing 
irrigation projects Government of India is extending central loan assistance to 
State Governments under Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme. The 
National Water Policy (1987) has been evaluated in the light of various 
shortcomings and emerging challenges including decline in water availability. The 
revised National Water Policy draft is now awaiting approval of the National Water 
Resources Council for adoption.

1777. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite large investments in irrigation only 
about 40 per cent of agricultural area is irrigated; 
(b) if so, the reasons for this state of affairs; 
(c) in what manner Government propose to generate irrigation potential 
to cover additional non-irrigated land; and 
(d) what has been the role of major and medium irrigation projects in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (d) 
Government of India has assessed the ultimate irrigation potential in the 
country as 139.9 million hectare (Mha.). The responsibility of investigation, 
planning, execution and maintenance of all types of irrigation projects/works 
primarily rests with the State Governments since irrigation is a State subject. 
Also, these irrigation projects/works are funded by the State Governments 
from their plan 
188 

[19 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
funds and according to their own prior ities. Creation of irrigation potential is 
a continuous process for which the target is set in th e State's Five Year Plans 
according to allocation of f unds by the States. At the beginning of the Ninth 
Five Year Plan, (i.e. 1997-98), 54.6 mha. was provided with irrigation 
against total sown area of 142.02 mha. which works out to 38.2 per cent. 
Creation of additional irrigation potential of about 10.2 mha. is expected 
during the Ninth Plan (1997—2002) thereby raising the total created irrigation 
potential to about 100 mha. of which the share of Major and Medium (M&M) 
projects is about 37.1 mha. 
Keeping in view the need to create additional irrigation potential, the 
Government has taken various policy and programme initiatives. These 
include creation of additional irrigation potential through new major, medium 
and minor irrigation projects; completion of ongoing projects; rehabilitation 
and modernisation of existing irrigation systems; restructuring and 
reorientation of the Command Area Development Programme; improving 
water management practices through Participatory Irrigation Management, 
promoting efficient and economic use of water for various purposes and 
laying emphasis on water conservation through various methods including use 
of latest technologies. 
In addition to allocations in the State Plans under the irrigation sector, 
Central Government is also providing financial assistance to the States in the 
form of loans under the Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme (AIBP), 
launched by the Central Government during 1996-97 for expeditious 
completion of ongoing major and medium irrigation projects. The scope of 
the programme was enhanced further during 1999-2000 by including minor 
irrigation schemes in respect of Special Category States, comprising the North-
Eastern States and Sikkim, Hilly States of J & K and Himachal Pradesh and 
drought prone Kalahandi, Bolangir, Koraput districts of Orissa. The Central 
Government has released Rs. 7876.74 crores to the State Governments under 
the scheme upto the end of February, 2002. It has also been decided to 
provide financial assistance to identified major/medium projects in an 
advanced stage of construction, which can be completed in one year (2 
working seasons) 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2002] 
under the Fast Track Programme with 100  per cent loan assistance. Priority 
will be given to pre-Fifth Plan and Fifth Plan projects for inclusion in the 
Fast Track Programme.

SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Sir,

Rs.408.9 crores. The Union Minister of Rural Development has been 
requested to sanction, at least, 25,000 I AY houses additionally for the 
current year, as a special case for providing permanent shelter to the 
flood victims. The Chief Minister  of Andhra Pradesh has already 
written to the Minister in this regard on 26.10.2001. I, therefore, 
request the Union Government to take an early action in the matter 
and come to the rescue of the flood victims.

SHRI K. B. KRISHNA MURTHY (Karnataka): Hon. Chairman. 
Sir, I would like to point out, through this Special Mention, that a social 
catastrophe is in the offing in Kolar Gold Fields, a city in Karnataka, 
due to the negligence, maladministration, laxity and lack of innovation 
on the part of the management of the BGML and the Government of 
India. A great legacy is being reduced to shambles. "Little England', as 
it was known, this tiny hamlet, once bustling with life, was the creation

has produced 810 metric tonnes of gold. The Gold Company originally 
employed 12,000 workers, and, today , it employes 4,000 workers, a 
majority of whom belong to the SC/ST community. Every conceivable 
infrastructure the once prosperous  company owned is in doldrums 
now. The salaries have not been paid for the past 12 months.

33 miners.

Need to check violence of left Extremism

there is terrorist violence; and, on the other, there is communal 
conflagration in various parts of the country. Besides this, several 
States of our country are affected by left extremism. According to 
official sources, violence unleashed by left ideological groupings is 
more difficult to tackle than communal violence which is an 
instantaneous outburst of passion. This rising graph of left extremist 
violence has caused not only many casualties, but also huge 
destruction of national property like police stations, vehicles and 
equipment. In spite of a ban on these groups, the growing scale of 
violence clearly indicates that most of them have gone underground

being supplied to these insurgent grou ps in the North-Eastern States

extremism is virulent in Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, 
Chhattisgarh; besides, nine other States are also in the grip of left 
extremism. In spite of reimbursement of 50 per cent of the expenditure 
to the States and equipping the police with modern weapons and 
giving them training, there has been no let up in left extremist 
violence.

Financial Crisis in North-Eastem States 
SHRI W. ANGOU SINGH (Manipur): Sir, through this Special 
Mention, I want to draw the attent ion of the hon. Finance Minister to 
the serious financial crisis faced by the North-Eastem States. Seven 
Sisters of the North-Eastern R egion, namely, Assam, Manipur, 
Nagaland, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh 
provide a colourful spectrum of rainbow to India. But the region is 
facing a number of problems, and ther e is a growing feeling that the 
people are yet to be drawn into the mainstream of India. Slowly, these 
States are now getting back on the rails. Formerly, the main problem of 
this region was its economic backwardness. This economic 
backwardness has created insurgency, and, now, a serious chronic 
disease has spread throughout the regi on. The situation is so critical 
that due to the financial crisis, the States do not release their share of 
funds for Central programmes and are unable to submit utilisation 
certificates to enable further release of Central funds. So, in the case 
of most of the programmes, even 50 pe r cent of the allocation is not 
fulfilled. 
In Manipur, the State's borrowing and total liability is rising 
steadily, and its overdraft was for 305 day from April, 2001 to February 
2002 as against 281 days' overdraft in the last financial year 2000-
2001. The State is sliding into a debt-trap where current borrowings 
are not enough even to finance the repayment of principal and interest. 
The State Government has taken various financial measures, with the 
signing of a MOU with the Government of India, but the recycling of 
funds for development expenditure is impossible and it is finding it 
difficult to obtain further instalments from the Centre. 
So, Sir, I urge upon the Finance Minister to take some specific 
financial policy measures, particularl y, for the North-Eastem States; 
either to write off the existing overdr aft of these States, as a one time 
grant, or to convert it into a long-term loan so as to enable each State 
to recycle its funds.

Serious problem to be created by the restriction of UAE Government on 
non-metric job seekers from India 
SHRI M.P. ABDUSSAMAD SAMADANI (Kerala): Mr. 
Chairman, I draw the attention of this august House to the serious 
problem going to be created due to the reported move of the UAE 
Government not to issue new job perm its to expatriates who lack High 
School qualification. The UAE reportedly wants to phase out such 
immigrants over three years. This will hit a large number of people from 
India especially from Kerala who work  in the UAE. Sir, according to a 
study the total number of Keralites in  the UAE is more than 4,05,000.

majority of Indians who work in t he Gulf countries though not metrics 
but are skilled and experienced in technical and other fields. Sir, 
already the condition of job opportunities in the Gulf is not so good. 
Many Gulf countries are restricting the entry of foreigners who seek 
jobs in their land. Our people are compelled to go abroad leaving their 
families and motherland for their livelihood due to the serious problem 
of unemployment that we face in our country. If enforced the proposed 
rules would not only restrict the iss ue of fresh visas to non-metrics but 
also prohibit renewal of work-permits to the existing non-matric 
employees thereby forcing a large number of Indians in UAE to return 
to the country. This could lead to serious socio-economic problems. 
Sir, already the State of Kerala is facing a serious economic problem. 
The exodus from the UAE would be a blow not only to the State of 
Kerala but numberless families who depend on the expatriates. I 
request the Government especially the External Affairs Minister 
through you, Sir, to urgently use our good relations with the UAE and 
our persuasive skills to make the friendly country desist from the 
reported restrictions.

BUDGET (GENERAL) 2002-2003 - Contd. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL (Bihar): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I consider it my 
privilege to rise and participate in the discussion on the Budget of 
2002-2003. Before I go on to the specifics, I would like to make some 
preliminary observations. Mr. Chairman, Sir, over the years, the annual 
budgetary exercise has not only become an exercise in finance but 
has also become a very sensitive exer cise in politics. Once, there is a 
coalition Government in power, with a large number of partners, the 
budgetary exercise takes its colour from different ideologies of the 
coalition partners. Therefore, it t ends to hamper the free play, that is 
required of the Finance Minister, in making budgetary allocations and 
giving a direction to the Budget. In this context, Sir, I consider it 
exceptionally important on the part of the political parties to start 
evolving a consensus on major economic issues, which our nation is 
faced with, the issues which are required to be addressed urgently and 
need to be resolved, as quickly as possible. Because, if this is not 
done, then, the world would leave us st anding by.   Unfortunately, that 
exercise in 
248 

[19 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
political consensus building has not developed, or, has not matured to 
the extent that one w ould have wanted. I hope that, in the years to 
come - and I do not expect any particular party to be in absolute 
majority -- this road will be taken by us, and, hopefully, we will start 
addressing certain basic issues. In 1991, with the new era of 
liberalisation we would have moved ahead. Unfortunately, as regards 
the first and the second generation reforms, I would like to say that the 
second generation reforms have not really started in a substantial 
way. Even the first generation ec onomic reforms have not really 
fructified. Another unfortunate thing that is developing in every 
budgetary process, and which has now become an annual feature is 
that, at the time of the Budget Speech, certain estimates are thought 
of, or, projected either relating to revenue collection or to expenditure; 
whether it relates to collection of customs duty or excise duty. When 
those budgetary figures are set out , certain amount of solemnity 
should be involved in those figures.  But I have seen over the years, 
and I do not really mean it as a criticism of any individual, that that 
solemnity of the budgetary figures, that solemnity of the budgetary 
estimates has somehow been looked upon with a sense of cynicism 
which has developed over the year s. The reason being that, perhaps, 
most of the estimates that are give n in the Budget really do not bear 
fruition. There is a lot of hype involved, there is a lot of wishful thinking 
involved, there is a lot of hope involved, but when you actually face the 
reality, at the end of the financial year, you find that the estmates have 
not fructified at all. 
Therefore, the ordinary man on th e street has started thinking 
of the Budgetary process in very cynical terms. He believes that these 
are only estimates, these are only figures, perhaps, for some 
byelections --perhaps, for some coming elections - and, that, in reality, 
the ordinary lot of the common man is not going to improve at all. I 
think, we need to address both these issues, namely, the issue of 
consensus, and the issue of increasing cynicism amongst the common 
folk of this country. 
Having made these preliminary observations, Sir, I would like 
to make two further points, and, i.e., that, in any Budget, there are two 
aspects that have to be looked at. One is the allocations made in the 
Budget; and the second is, which is, even more important, the 
direction that the Finance Minister or the Government of the day is 
going to give to the economy. I think, one is as important as the other, 
because one really is a reflection of the other in some ways. Now, 
when you talk of Budgetary allocations or economic direction, you 
have to think in terms of short-term 
249 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2002] 
problems that we have to meet with, and, then, of course, the long-
term problems that we have to meet with. Now, if we look at the 
economic situation, last year, Mr. Chairman, Sir, the one thing on 
which everybody is agreed -- I think, the RBI Governor has also made 
a statement to that effect; economists have written time and again in 
different newspapers; various business houses, FICCI, and very many 
other organisations, have agreed on one issue -- is that the real 
problem with our economy today "Ts the complete absence of 
demand, and this is reflected in the slow rates of growth. Therefore, 
the task of the Finance Minister, in  this context, has to be to devise 
ways and means to give impetus to that demand. Sir, I jus* want to 
place a few figures before the hon. Me mbers of this House. Th6 real 
consumption growth decreased from 6.5 per cent in 1999-2000 to 2.9 
per cent in 2000-01. The Government consumption expenditure 
decreased during the same period from 12 per cent to 6.5 per cent. 
The tax revenues have fallen much short of the budgetary estimates. 
There is a fall in sales and profits all around in the corporate sector, 
and though the Government must be c ongratulating itself as the large 
foreign exchange reserves, as well as the large stocks of foodgrains, I 
do not think that it is an indi cation of sound fundamentals, sound 
economic fundamentals. In fact, this situation represents a situation of 
low income and demand, resulting in low input and low off-take of 
foodgrains. In fact, the hon. Finance Minister very well knows that the 
stock of foodgrains Is 58 million tonne s, as of today, — In fact, as of 
January, 2002 - as against the required stock of 16.8 million tonnes. 
And, of course, the accumulation of stocks has resulted in increased 
expenditure for retaining these stoc ks. The economic cost of storing 
wheat has increased from Rs. 584 per quintal in 1995-96 to Rs. 839 
per quintal in 2001-02. The economic cost of storing rice has increased 
from Rs. 763 per quintal in 1995-96 to Rs. 1174 per quintal in 2001-02. 
So, any individual, any economist, analysing this situation, will realise 
that the basic problem with the I ndian economy is the purchasing 
power of the ordinary man. And it is unfortunate that whereas we have 
a large stock of foodgrains on the one hand, on the other, we have a 
large section of the Indian community  living in utter poverty, not even 
being able to lift the stocks that are available, at relatively cheaper 
prices. Therefore, I want to reiterat e what I stated. What is required, 
rather, what was required of the Finance Minister was to inject demand 
into the economy, by taking such fiscal measures as would result in 
that. Also, there should be an increase in public expenditure to create 
a kind of atmosphere to increase t he demand. Unfortunately, some of 
the steps that are required to be taken in this regard

just want to point out some figures  for the last year to show how, 
sometimes, the budgetary allocations never meet the objectives. Take, 
for example, the figures for this y ear. This year the Budget increases 
the Capital Account Expenditure on agriculture from Rs.66.45 crores to 
Rs.85.66 crores. I have to say that it is a substantial increase. 
Sir, if we look at the last year's figures, the budgetary 
allocation for the capital account on agriculture sector was Rs. 66.45 
crores. But, what was the amount actually spent? It was only Rs. 
50.19 crores. What does it mean? It means, even if you make 
increased allocations for the agriculture sector in your Budget, the 
reality is that the money will not be spent. If you have increased the 
allocation for the capital account on the agriculture sector from Rs. 66 
crores to Rs. 85 crores, I am afraid, at the end of the

year, this money will not be spent because you will be again afraid of 
your fiscal deficit. Therefore, it is necessary, as I said, to give a 
direction in your Budget to increase demand, to increase public 
expenditure. I am afraid, with the state of financial institutions of this 
country, with the state of finances of this country where fiscal deficit is 
now projected as 5.7 per cent, I am not sure, whether any substantial 
amount of public expenditure is going to be made to increase the kind 
of demand that is necessary to boost the economy. That is what is 
really missing in the Budget. There are no attempts to boost the 
economy. Of course, we have gone for a higher dosage of excise for 
the purpose of getting more revenue. There has been an increase in 
the excise duty with excise propo sals leading to a revenue gain of Rs.

last year, I do not even think that these figures would be realised. But, 
in fact, this increase in excise is going to aggravate the problems of 
business. As it is, business is doing very badly. As you know, industrial 
output is down; all the sectors of the economy are down. This" 
increase in excise duty will put more burden on the poor. What 
happens if the excise duty is increa sed? The Finance Minister knows 
very well that everything is passed on to the poor men, to the ordinary 
consumers. This is not going to lead to any boost in the demand. On 
the other hand, though mere has been an increase in the excise duty 
for whatever reasons, perhaps, because of WTO, and the customs 
duty has been reduced. There is a revenue loss of Rs. 2,000 crores.

man. There is going to be a redu ction in the customs duty. If the 
performance of the last year's Budget is any projection of what is going 
to happen next year, there is again going to be a decrease in revenue, 
there is again going to be a decrease in expenditure. So, where is the 
economy going? Which direction is the economy taking? The central 
problem, as I said, has not been addressed by the hon. Finance 
Minister. In fact, I was very impr essed last time when the Finance 
Minister talked about fiscal responsibility and how the economy had to 
be subjected to constraints by the Government in respect of its 
expenditure. In fact, the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management 
Bill was introduced in the Lok S abha in 2000. What does clause 4(1) of 
the Bill say? It says, "The Central Government shall take appropriate 
measures to eliminate revenue deficit and fiscal deficit and build up 
adequate revenue surplus".  Where is the surplus?

the generality of the foregoing provisions, the Central Government 
should reduce fiscal deficit for a financial year to not more than 2 per 
cent of the estimated GDP for that year within a period of five financial 
years beginning from the initial financial year on 1 81 April, 2001 and

deficit has grown to 5.7 per cent. The fact of the matter is, unless the 
economy grows at the rate of 8 per  cent per annum, we are not going

means, a domestic investment and savi ngs rate of 30 per cent  of the 
GDP.

as a percentage of GDP, declined from 24.8 per cent in 1994-95 to

nowhere near the eight per cent ma rk. And, your Budget and your 
policies are not even looking towards that direction.

Finance Minister has, time and again, I appreciate his sentiments - 
said that there is a need to improv e fiscal discipline by the States, and 
he has announced a number of schemes for reform-linked funding in 
several sectors such as power and urban development, as also the

three posts of Secretaries of the Fi nance Ministry. Abolish three posts

adoption of zero-base budgeting has remained merely a slogan on 
paper. Sir, the Expenditure Reforms Commission has submitted ten

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: I have perfect understanding 
and harmony with my colleagues. Sir, I rise to support the Budget 
presented by the hon. Finance Minister. Sir, I was privileged to speak 
on the Motion of Thanks to the President's address a couple of days 
back, in which I have stated certain realities of the economy that are 
being faced by us. I should congratulate the Finance Minister for doing 
a very good exercise, in spite of all the constraints that he is facing. It 
is not that I am congratulating the Finance Minister to win over his 
favour. I am speaking about the ground reality. Our economy has got 
its own strength. It has got some in built strength, that is, surplus 
foodgrains, foreign exchange reserves and low rate of inflation. At the 
same time,  it has got its own weaknesses, that is, 
265 

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2002]  
growing fiscal deficit and revenue de ficit, declining contribution to the 
GDP from agriculture, social dish armony in the country and low tax 
GDP ratio. Sir, I want to dwell on two important subjects. I have been 
speaking continuously on the floor of the House that with all the evils 
that are being faced by the economy, the contribution of the agriculture 
to GDP has to be increased. It was earlier 40 per cent. Now, it has 
been reduced to 25 per cent; and at this juncture, I cannot see any 
other panacea other than the agriculture to cure this problem. You see, 
it is a zinda tilsmaat for our economy. The first area of the adverse 
impact on the declining contribution to the GDP is employment. 
Seventy per cent of our population still lives on 25 per cent of the GDP, 
and 62 per cent of the workforce is from agriculture. Unless you 
improve the economic standards of the majority of people, there will 
not be aggregate demands for goods. Sir, the fact is that I am not 
blaming the NDA Government al one for all these ills. We have 
inherited some problems, as a legacy, from the earlier regimes. So, 
what I am trying to appeal to all the political parties is that let us have 
the courage to sit together and discuss these issues. I am sorry to say 
that there is no debate on the econ omy; but there is a debate on so 
many trivial issues. There should be a debate on the economy. It is 
very easy to criticise and make a political capital out of it. But, people 
are very intelligent. Let us have a consensus on the economic policies 
that have to be adopted in this country , keeping in view the constraints 
and the imbalances that the economy is facing. Sir, any country which 
has to be developed, social harmony should be there. I do not want to 
go into the details of the temple issue or other issues which have been 
discussed very exhaustively in this House. It has become a vexatious 
issue. We do not need temples or mosques or any place of worship, 
which will create disharmony in this country, which will create 
disturbance in the societ y, which will mar the prestige of the country. 
As had once been described by the late Prime Minister, Pandit 
Jawaharlal Nehru, in order to build up this country, we need modern 
temples like the hydro-electric and irrigation projects of Bhakra Nangal 
and Nagarjuna Sagar. We need temples like that so that we can 
improve the productivity of the farm ers. We can improve the wealth of 
the nation by providing basic infrastructure to agriculture and industry. 
We need such temples, not the temple s that will create disturbance in 
the society and hamper the growth of the nation. 
Sir, there is one more aspect which I want to emphasise.   In 
fact, a thrust has to be given to the agriculture.     I have been saying 
this all

[19 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
along. Today, 49 per cent of the ur ban poor and 42 per cent of the 
rural poor are undernourished to t he extent of 25 per cent. We are 
unable to feed our population. This  has been confirmed by the report 
of the World Health Organisation. How can we expect the people to 
create demand for goods, when they are not able to fill their own 
bellies, which is the basic necessity for their survival? First, we have to 
cater to the needs of the masses. We need production by the masses,

strong protagonist of reforms; reform s that are suited to the needs of 
the nation, to the needs of the people. That is what we needed. We 
don't need a tailor-made or ready-made formula to be implemented 
here, as has been implemented somewhere. Our culture is different. 
Our needs are different. We have got one billion population. The entire 
condition that prevails in this country is different. Shri Pranab 
Mukherjee stated certain facts. I, t oo, mentioned those facts a couple 
of days ago. In spite of having surplus foodgrains in the godowns, 
there have been starvation deaths. Why is it happening? It is because, 
and I emphasise, that 70 per cent  of the masses do not have the 
money, the purchasing capacity, to purchase the basic necessities. 
That is why there is a glut in the market and a surplus in the godowns. 
We are unable to dispose it of. All along, we have been more 
accustomed to solving the problems of  deficit. The issue of surplus is 
a new phenomenon in this country. The Government is yet to come 
out with a mechanism, to deal with it. The traditional buyers of 
foodgrains from our country have become self-sufficient. A major 
chunk of the population is unable to purchase the foodgrains from our 
godowns. So, there is no offtake. This is the dichotomy. This has to be 
addressed. The Government should show the sagacity to face the 
challenges that are being posed before this country. Instead of doing 
that, the Government has become a silent spectator. I am sorry to 
state that. The Government should come out and face them bravely. 
After all, growth of the economy is of paramount importance for this 
country. I admit, in the first three years of post-reforms period, there 
was a growth rate of 6.5 per cent to  7 per cent. But, it was, virtually, a 
jobless growth. There was stagnation in the growth of employment in 
the agricultural sector because of  the declining contribution by the 
agricultural sector, which was not compensated by the incremental 
increase in employment in the indu strial and service sectors. Today, 
56 per cent of the GDP is being enjo yed by the 10 per cent employed 
in the service sector and the 20 per  cent industrial workforce are 
enjoying 20 per cent of the

RAJYA SABHA [19 March, 2002]  
GDP. If you remove the 10 per cent of the top 10 corporate bodies in

the Preamble of the Constitution, that we would eradicate the 
economic inequalities. Let us not build ocean of poverty amidst island

economic policies are contributing to this aspect. Now, I will come to

targets have remained totally unachiev ed. We could not achieve these 
targets. Whether it is the export sector or the agriculture sector or the 
industrial sector, we have not been able to achieve the targets 
because of obvious reasons which are prevailing today. Today, I read 
a news item in the newspapers. The Governor of the Reserve Bank of 
India predicted a growth rate of 6. 5 per cent. I do not know how it will 
be achieved because today, the growth rate is between 5.1 per cent 
and 5.2 per cent. It is very doubtful. If you want to improve the growth 
rate by 1.5 per cent, what is the addi tional infrastructure that has been 
created? You need further investments. The Government has not been 
able to get savings, as Shri Kapil Sibal mentioned. Shri Kapil Sibal 
said, "There should be 35 per cent savings." I say that there should be 
38 per cent savings of the GDP. Unless you mop up public savings, 
there will not be public investment in  the infrastructure sector. Unless 
there is public investment, there will be no private investment because 
there is a strong complementarity between public investment and 
private investment which creates demand for goods, which kicks back 
the economy. This problem has not been addressed to in this Budget 
also. 
Sir, I would like to mention one more thing. I would like to 
quote from the C&AG report, 2000. The total capital expenditure in the 
year 1999-2000 was as low as Rs. 29023 crores. The public 
perception is that whatever amount  has been classified as capital 
expenditure would go for creation of capital assets. But, it is not true. 
Whatever capital expenditure has been classified, is not for creating 
capital assets. Capital expenditure of Rs. 29023 crores for the year 
1999-2000 constitutes 7 per cent of the total overall expenditure. It is a 
miserable thing. Out of the total expenditure, we are spending only 7 
per cent towards the capital expenditure.    Out of

balance Rs. 23,000 crores is for the Non-Plan Expenditure. So, only 
Rs. 6,000 crores is being spent to create capital assets. How to 
address this mounting problem in this country? Things are not going to 
be any different in the current year or  in the years to come, given that 
the revenue deficit continues to be a major proportion of fiscal deficit. 
In the year 2000-2001, the total expenditure is Rs. 3,25,611 crores and

goes to the non-Plan. Only two to three per cent of the total 
expenditure is being spent towards capital expenditure which is meant 
for capital assets creation. This is the sorry state of affairs which is 
prevailing in this country. The CA G Report further points out that 
during the last six years of the Plan expenditure, while the revenue 
expenditure has been growing at 14.43 per cent, the capital 
expenditure has been growing only at the rate of 2.86 per cent. See 
the disparity, the imbalance in th e economy, the structural changes 
which need to be addressed by the Government, Further, it has been 
noticed that in absolute terms, the capital expenditure, as a part of the 
Plan expenditure, is coming down. So, the asset creation is worsening

being inhibited by the dwindling allocations for capital expenditure, and 
there is little hope for revival of the economy, notwithstanding any 
number of policy initiatives that may be taken by the Government for 
giving a boost to the economy. As I have said earlier, I cannot blame 
the NDA Government for the present fiscal problems confronting the 
nation. I would like to appeal - it is a whole-hearted appeal that I am 
making to all the political parties - to everybody; let us sit together, 
discuss and debate what sort of a policy is needed for this country, to 
revive the economy, to improve the strength of-the nation, so" that our 
one billion population will have two square meals a day and can live 
peacefully and happily in the societ y without any disturbance. Let us 
discuss and formulate a policy which is suitable to this country. 
Sir, there are some anomalies which have crept into our 
economy. Even though my Leftist friends would object to it, Sir, I 
should say that the Fifth Pay Commission has played a very 
devastating role on the economy. About Rs. 36,000 crores had to be 
borrowed by the Government in order to implement the Fifth Pay 
Commission Report; and, putting the burden of all

SHRI P. N. SIVA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, the fifth Budget presented

and growth in one package. Sharing his high hopes, we expect that his 
strategy will work out successfully. The first welcome point is that there 
is no change in the Income-tax rates. But, while the poorer sections 
barely find a mention in the Budget, the middle class, driving force 
behind the industrial boom in recent years has been further 
impoverished through the 5% Income-tax surcharge on grounds of 
Defence, even though a war has not broken out actually. However, the 
2% surcharge on account of Gujarat has been withdrawn, and we 
thank the Finance Minister for that. 
There are certain new proposals  that are to be appreciated 
and welcomed, especially the setting up  of the Agricultural Insurance 
Corporation, the Employment Guar antee Schemes in poorer districts 
and the Jana Raksha Health Insurance Scheme for the poor. In this 
connection, I would like to state that when we were ruling in Tamil 
Nadu, our State Government had implemented a scheme called the 
'Varmunkapom', based on the theory that prevention is better than 
cure. The Government reached out to the poor people and they were 
treated free of cost. Having the ex perience of that scheme, I can 
expect how this scheme can help the people. So, it is the bounden 
duty of everyone to appreciate it. The new contributory pension 
scheme for new recruits in Government is one which I cannot 
understand, because there is already a ban on recruitment. How far 
this scheme would help those who would be recruited in future is a 
question mark. Then, power, roads, railways have got a Plan outlay of

amorphous package. There are indeed, a few more initiatives. The 
biggest one is the Rs. 12,000 crores incentive-linked assistance for the

development reforms, rural infrastructure, power and irrigation. There 
is something also to be said as well for the large tax package for the

face a fierce global competition after quotas in the West are removed

the fatigue of the Finance Minister in presenting the fifth successive 
Budget. The Government has presented the Economic Survey for 
2002. The Economic Survey presents a very dismal picture. The 
growth rate would have been much less this year, but for the growth in 
the agriculture. The growth rate is 5.1 per cent as against the growth

performance of the agricultural sector. Otherwise, the growth rate 
would have been 3 per cent or less than 3 per cent. 
The hon. Finance Minister ih his Budget Speech has stated 
that he has made certain efforts to draw the strategy for the Budget. 
According to him, the agenda of t he Budget is to consolidate the 
economic reforms and give a boost to the second generation 
economic reforms. In,that proce ss, he has stated the thrust areas.

strengthening the financial sector  and capital market, regenerating 
industrial growth, providing social security to the poor and 
consolidating the tax reforms. 
I appreciate the efforts made by the Finance Minister. The 
steps which he has initiated to consolidate the second-generation 
reforms are quite laudable. But, when we look at the allocations, we 
get disappointed. How are you going to achieve the targets which have 
been fixed? The agriculture sector is a thrust area. Every Member has 
said that the agriculture sector is a thrust area because 70 per cent of 
our population is engaged in this sect or. If we look at the provisions 
made for the agriculture sector, this year, there is a marginal increase. 
Without proper investment we will not be able to achieve the growth 
which we are expecting or anticipating.  The same is the case with all 
the six thrust areas which the hon. Finance Minister has mentioned. 
Growth is not possible without infrastructure. Slow rate of infrastructure 
development, less investments in the Plan expenditure, more 
investments in non-Plan expenditure and cost overrun in the 
infrastructure sector are some of the problems which we are facing. 
The hon. Finance Minister has emphasised that there should be public 
and private investment in the infrastructure sector. But how can the 
private investment come? In the whole Budget speech, there ar$ no 
incentives for the private sector. Infrastructure has to be developed. 
But the public sector cannot develop it. The Finance Minister has 
admitted that it is not possible for the public sector to invest in the 
infrastructure sector. The privat e sector will not invest in the 
infrastructure, unless there are some incentives for the private sector. 
In the whole Budget speech there is nothing for the private sector.

banking sector. He has promised that he would bring in a Bill to 
revamp the SEBI; It is very essential and this must be done 
immediately. The SEBI has to be controlled and the SEBI's role should 
be to improve the capital market. Similarly, reforms in the banking 
sector are urgently needed. Today, bu lk of the savings is from the 
banking sector and if we don't revamp the banking sector, people's 
faith in the banking sector will go aw ay. The hon. Finance Minister has 
stated that a new Bill on the banking sector reforms is proposed to be 
introduced in Parliament to strengthen the credit rights, through a 
foreclosure enforcement of security, by banks and financiaJ 
institutions. So, there is a need for a comprehensive banking reforms. 
Whether it is the SEBI reforms or  the banking reforms, these have 
become bureaucratic reforms. There is no consultative process on all 
these reforms. Either the Reserve Ba nk or the Finance Ministry brings 
in the reforms. On the other hand,  there should be a detailed debate 
on the banking reforms. Experts in the banking sector have to be 
consulted; there should be a widespread discussion on how to bring 
about banking reforms; how there should be transparency in the 
banking operations and how the NPAs should be controlled.   For 
example, there is no consistency even in the formula to

be adopted in the matter of NPAs. First they say that if a loan is 
outstanding for 180 days, then, it should be taken as a NPA. But, later, 
the Reserve Bank brings it dow n to 90 days. Tnere are no clear 
policies on These matters. If some rule or the other keeps changing 
each and every time, then, there will be confusion. The banking 
reforms should have a wider acceptability in the banking sector. These 
days, the depositors are afraid to keep their money with the banks. 
The position in the banks, whether it is a nationalised bank or a private 
bank, is not good. So, there is a need for reassuring the depositors. A 
person does not know how and where he should put his savings. Even 
if he puts his money in the bank, he •s doubtful as to whether his 
money is safe there or not. If he invests in UTl, then again, he is 
doubtful whether he will get his money back. So, we have to properly 
regulate all these small savings, be it in banks or in mutual funds. In 
this connection, the Finance Mini ster has said that the Deposit 
insurance Credit Guarantee Corporation is going to be converted into 
a bank. Yes; today, the Deposit Insurance Credit Guarantee 
Corporation collects premium from all the banks on deposits, but 
restricts its clients to a particular amount. So, if the faith of the 
depositors in the banking sector is to be strengthened, there is a need 
today that the entire deposit should be insured The entire deposit has 
to be insured. If any financial institution or any bank gets into 
problems, the depositors should not be left in the lurch, and they 
should not be deprived of their savings. There is a need for urgent 
reforms and also a need for changing the perception of the Deposit 
Insurance Credit Guarantee Corporation; instead of insuring deposits 
only up to a particular limit, the entire deposits of the banks should be 
insured; and whenever any untoward thing happens, the depositors 
should not be made to suffer. 
Sir, my last point is about the.  tax reforms. There is absolutely 
no change in the tax reforms. The Finance Minister has said that he 
has not changed the tax rate; but a surcharge has been levied. Also, 
the rebate under section 88 has been reduced to 10% from 20%; I 
wonder why this change has been made. I would suggest that this 
20% should be maintained, because it is through that that savings are 
mobilised, whCher it is insurance or Provident Fund or the various 
other things. It is one of the incentives for savings. As it is, there is no 
incentive for savings in the entire Budget. We have all been saying 
that the rate of savings is very low. If we have to achieve a growth rate 
of 8%, then the rate of savings should be

As I mentioned earlier, resource mobilisation from the primary 
market has gone down from 56 per cent to just 5.5 per cent. This 
requires an urgent action, and the primary market has to be 
strengthened. Then, some of the term -lending institutions -- the IDBI,

For example, the SEBI's book-buildi ng method is solely responsible 
for the debacle in the stock market and in the UTI; and some of the 
unscrupulous companies, by resorti ng to this book-building method, 
have duped some of the public sector banks, hiking the prices of 
shares, and then making the ordinary investor lose heavily. 
So, there should be a second thought whether the Unit Trust

method. In my view, it should not be resorted to, particularly, by the 
funding institutions, because the ba nks and the investing institutions 
should not invest through the priv ate placement method. Sir, with 
these few remarks, I thank you for giving me an opportunity to 
participate on the discussion on the General Budget.
